catalog_quote: [Pulipaty 2019] The elusive nature of Telugu stress ... Previous works on Telugu word stress (Sitapati 1936; Sailaja 1985) postulate: Primary stress falls on the first syllable; But if the first syllable is light and the second heavy, it falls on the second syllable. However, a study on auditory perception of Telugu stress by Lisker and Krishnamurti (1991) finds contradictory results: Little consistency in stress judgements of speakers; A somewhat noticeable pattern is that the second syllable carries stress; The first syllable stressed only if it contained a long vowel and if the second syllable contained a short vowel ... new_statements.quote: "Primary stress in Telugu goes on the heavier of the first two syllables in a word. Secondary stress goes on every alternate mora starting from the primary stressed syllable unless it is final. In heavy syllables (CVC, CVV, CVVC), stress goes on the initial mora." (p. 12) | "This is the primary stress rule reported in previous work (Sitapati, 1936; Pingali, 1985)- stress the second syllable if it is heavy, otherwise the first" (p. 10) | "In a non-compound word, if the vowel in the second syllable is long and the vowel in the first is short, the second syllable receives the stress. In all other cases, the first syllable receives the stress." (p. 46, Pingali 1985 after Sitapati 1936)
new_statements.citation: Kolachina, Sudheer. 2016. Stress and vowel harmony in Telugu. MA thesis, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MITWPL).
new_statements.locator: pp. 12, 10 (with fn. 5), and Appendix 'Stress' pp. 46-47 (printed page numbers = PDF pages 12, 10, 46-47); also p. 4 (introduction) and p. 36 (conclusions)
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Telugu (catalog-all-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so this supplies the placement: weight-sensitive within the first two syllables (heavier of the first two, default initial), plus a secondary-stress statement. Nothing to contradict; the source itself is explicit that the rule is assumed from Sitapati 1936/Pingali 1985 rather than phonetically established.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the heavier of the first two syllables: on the second syllable if it is heavy and the first is light, otherwise on the first. Kolachina counts CVC, CVV and CVVC (and VC, VV, CVCC; p. 25) as heavy; the older Sitapati (1936)/Pingali (1985) formulation that he adopts (pp. 46-47) is stated in terms of vowel length only (long second vowel after short first vowel takes the stress). He also notes (p. 10 fn. 5, p. 47) that this is the same primary-stress rule as Malayalam (Mohanan 1986; Hayes 1995: 92-93, moraic trochee with no degenerate feet), and that stress can equivalently be stated as left-to-right moraic-trochee parsing (p. 4).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on every alternate mora counting from the primary-stressed syllable, never on a final mora (pp. 4, 12, 36); in heavy syllables stress sits on the first mora (p. 12). Inferred from resistance to vowel harmony; a production experiment (section 5, pp. 30-35) found syllable duration significantly higher in the secondary-stress position (HLL) than in the unstressed position (LLL), though vowel duration and mean intensity showed no significant effect (p. 35-36). Sitapati (1936) also reports secondary stress in compounds on the prominent syllable of the second element (p. 46).
new_statements.exceptions: Kolachina flags that 'Previous work on Telugu phonology contains differing claims about the stress system' (p. 46): Krishnamurti (2003: 59-60) found speaker variation for CVCVCV stems, with about twice as many subjects judging the second syllable of [palaka] 'slate' stressed as the first (p. 47); Balusu (2001) found duration and F0 reliable, loudness/intensity poor cues to primary stress (pp. 31, 47); 'further phonetic studies are required to clearly establish the facts about the vowel system and stress patterns in Telugu. In this thesis, I assume the stress rules of Sitapati (1936) reported by Pingali (1985)' (p. 47). Light-first + long-second-vowel shapes (the second-syllable-stress case) are mostly Sanskrit/Perso-Arabic loans; in native stems a long second vowel co-occurs with a heavy first syllable (p. 46). Stems containing a suffix or post-position, and compounds, are excluded from the non-compound rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Kolachina 2016 does not name a dialect in the passages read; his data are corpus/dictionary stems and a production experiment with Telugu speakers at MIT. The wrong-item for work 0 (Krishnamurti & Gumperz 1961/62) describes 'Modern Telugu' (standard written/spoken). No work describes a regional variety.

readall_conflicts: The only work opened in full, Kolachina 2016, states a weight-sensitive rule (heavier of the first two syllables, else initial; secondary stress on alternate moras) but explicitly says the literature disagrees: Krishnamurti 2003: 59-60 (not opened; reported at Kolachina p. 47) found speaker variation with a second-syllable preference for CVCVCV [palaka], and Kolachina adopts the Sitapati 1936/Pingali 1985 rule as an assumption pending phonetic work (p. 47; p. 31 'There is little clarity on what the exact acoustic correlates of primary stress in Telugu are'). Two items already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 pass but not in this works list point the same way: Lisker & Krishnamurti 1991 (ICPhS XII, 'Lexical stress in a "stressless" language') report that neither Telugu nor English listeners 'showed any strong preference for selecting initial syllables as the bearers of primary stress. If anything, the penultimate syllable was somewhat more often chosen' (p. 90), and Nagamma Reddy 1999 (ICPhS) says 'Duration in Telugu functions as stress does across languages'. So the weight-sensitive placement is the descriptive tradition (Sitapati, Pingali, Kolachina, and Aitha 2026 NLLT presupposes foot-based stress), while the experimental tradition (Lisker & Krishnamurti; Krishnamurti 2003) finds stress judgements unstable and no clear initial default. The Steever 1998 chapter and the IEL&L 2026 chapter could not be opened, so their positions are unknown.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote check passes on all three locators. The classification (weight-hedged, left-edge two-syllable window, default initial) rests on a 2019 AMP poster carrying Sitapati 1936/Sailaja 1985/Kolachina 2016 second-hand; the held primaries (K&G 1985 reference grammar, JIPA 2017, SPA 1979, and now Lisker 1963) are silent on stress position or deny only contrastive stress. The newly downloaded Lisker & Krishnamurti 1991 (first-hand, replacing the poster's paraphrase) refines rather than overturns: it confirms 'no contrastive stress', reports no initial preference, a penult/second-syllable tendency in all-light trisyllables, trochaic all-light disyllables, and a weak preference for the last long vowel, with Telugu listeners near-random - i.e. exactly the contest that motivates the tentative classification; it does not support a categorical left-window rule but also does not establish a different one. Nothing
